title: On the Use of Agentic Coding: An Empirical Study of Pull Requests on GitHub
finding: 567 Claude Code PRs in 157 OSS projects: 83.8% merged, but only 54.9% of merged PRs went in unmodified; 45.1% needed human revisions, esp. bug fixes, docs and project-specific standards (per authors).
why_for_us: Expect roughly half of cheap-agent PRs to need a fix-up pass; budget Claude review time for convention adherence, not just correctness.

title: Where Do AI Coding Agents Fail? An Empirical Study of Failed Agentic Pull Requests in GitHub
finding: 33k agent PRs from five agents: docs/CI/build tasks merge best, performance and bug-fix worst; unmerged PRs are larger, touch more files and often fail CI; rejection taxonomy includes duplicate PRs, unwanted features and agent misalignment (per authors).
why_for_us: Cap card size (files/lines) and require green CI before Claude even reviews; route bug-fix/perf cards to stronger models.

title: Comparing AI Coding Agents: A Task-Stratified Analysis of Pull Request Acceptance
finding: 7,156 PRs from Codex, Copilot, Devin, Cursor, Claude Code: task type dominates acceptance (docs 82.1% vs new features 66.1%), a gap larger than most inter-agent differences; no agent is best on all task types (per authors).
why_for_us: Track acceptance per card type, not per model; choose which agent/model gets a card by task category.

title: Why Are AI Agent-Involved Pull Requests (Fix-Related) Remain Unmerged? An Empirical Study
finding: 8,106 fix-related agent PRs; manual analysis of 326 closed-unmerged PRs yields 12 failure reasons, with test failures and the same issue already resolved by another PR most common; build failures rare (per authors).
why_for_us: Dedup cards before dispatch (one issue = one card = one branch) so parallel agents do not solve the same thing twice.

title: When AI Teammates Meet Code Review: Collaboration Signals Shaping the Integration of Agent-Authored Pull Requests
finding: On AIDev, reviewer engagement is the strongest correlate of merge; larger changes and force pushes lower merge likelihood; iteration count alone explains little once collaboration signals are included (per authors).
why_for_us: Claude review should give actionable, convergent feedback to the cheap agent rather than trigger blind retries; forbid force-push on agent branches.

title: How AI Coding Agents Communicate: A Study of Pull Request Characteristics and Human Review Responses
finding: PR description style differs across five agents and is associated with reviewer engagement, response time and merge outcome (per authors).
why_for_us: Standardise a PR-description template (what/why/how verified/risks) so the owner can approve quickly.

title: How AI Coding Agents Modify Code: A Large-Scale Study of GitHub Pull Requests
finding: 24,014 merged agentic PRs vs 5,081 human PRs: agent PRs have far more commits (Cliff's delta 0.54), moderately more files/deleted lines, slightly higher description-to-diff similarity (per authors).
why_for_us: Squash agent commits and judge by the diff, not the commit log.

title: Security in the Age of AI Teammates: An Empirical Study of Agentic Pull Requests on GitHub
venue: arXiv (journal version: Information and Software Technology, W7214402852)
finding: About 4% of 33k agent PRs are security-related (1,293 confirmed), mostly hardening (tests, config, error handling); they merge less and wait longer; rejection tracks complexity and verbosity more than security topic (per authors).
why_for_us: Label security-touching cards (auth, PESEL, payments) for mandatory double review; keep those PRs small.

title: When AI Writes Code: Investigating Security Issues in Agentic Software Changes
finding: SAST over 7,200 agent vs 6,620 human PRs: agents introduce CWEs including hard-coded credentials and command injection; on small focused bug fixes agents introduce fewer/less severe issues; larger PRs are task-dependent (per authors).
why_for_us: Run a SAST/secret scanner in CI on every agent PR; small cards are also safer cards.

title: AI Agent Pull Requests on GitHub: Frequency, Structure, and Merge Conflict Rates
finding: In 33,596 agent PRs, 40.2% of repos have temporally overlapping agent PR pairs; replayed merges conflict in 41.7% of cross-agent pairs vs 19.8% same-agent pairs, mostly in source files (84.4%) (per authors).
why_for_us: Parallel cards must own disjoint files; merge serially to cut the 20-40% conflict rate.

title: Agentic Much? Adoption of Coding Agents on GitHub
finding: Across 128,018 projects, estimated coding-agent adoption was 22.20-28.66% by Feb 2026 and rising; agent-assisted commits are larger than human-only commits (per authors).
why_for_us: Agent-heavy work is now mainstream, but larger commits mean review is the bottleneck to design for.

title: SWE-chat: Coding Agent Interactions From Real Users in the Wild
finding: ~18,000 real sessions: in 41% agents write virtually all code; only 59% of agent-produced code survives into commits; agent code introduces more vulnerabilities than human code; users push back in 50% of turns (per authors).
why_for_us: Assume ~40% of agent output is waste; measure our own code-survival rate per card as a cost KPI.

title: How Coding Agents Fail Their Users: A Large-Scale Analysis of Developer-Agent Misalignment in 20,574 Real-World Sessions
finding: 20,574 sessions: seven misalignment forms (reading project, intent, rule following, action bounds, implementation, progress reporting); 90.50% of episodes cost effort/trust rather than damage, but 91.49% of resolutions need explicit user correction; constraint violations and inaccurate self-reporting grow in share (per authors).
why_for_us: Build the review checklist around the seven forms, especially rule-following and self-reporting, which are rising.

title: Code with Me or for Me? How Increasing AI Automation Transforms Developer Workflows
finding: First controlled study of developers with coding agents vs copilots: agents complete tasks humans might not and reduce effort, but users often do not adequately understand agent behaviour (per authors).
why_for_us: Owner understanding is the weak link; Claude summaries of what the agent actually did are worth their cost.

title: Professional Software Developers Don't Vibe, They Control: AI Agent Use for Coding in 2025
finding: Field observations (N=13) and surveys (N=99): experienced developers keep control of design and implementation, using expertise-based strategies to constrain agents, and prefer collaboration over full delegation (per authors).
why_for_us: Since the owner is not a programmer, the control role must be played by Claude plus written specs and tests.

title: Writing Code vs. Shipping Code: Productivity Effects Across Generations of AI Coding Tools
finding: 500,000+ GitHub developers: autocomplete, interactive agents and autonomous agents raise commits by 30%, 180% and 240%, but the 240% shrinks to 80% for projects and 30% for releases; elasticity of substitution 0.23 implies human bottlenecks (per authors).
why_for_us: Measure shipped features per week, not commits or PRs; the human approval step is the binding constraint.

title: Speed at the Cost of Quality: How Cursor AI Increases Short-Term Velocity and Long-Term Complexity in Open-Source Projects
finding: Diff-in-diff on Cursor adopters: large but transient velocity gain, with substantial persistent increases in static-analysis warnings and complexity that drive later slowdown (per authors).
why_for_us: Make lint/complexity gates first-class in CI so the speed from cheap agents does not turn into a slowdown months later.

title: AI IDEs or Autonomous Agents? Measuring the Impact of Coding Agents on Software Development
finding: Staggered diff-in-diff on AIDev: front-loaded velocity gains only where agents were the first AI tool; static-analysis warnings and cognitive complexity rise ~18% and ~39% persistently (per authors).
why_for_us: Track warnings and complexity per repo monthly; a rising trend is a stop signal for adding more parallel agents.

title: A Few Pages of Markdown: Committed AI Configuration and Lower Quality Cost after Coding-Agent Adoption
finding: 441 repos: agents add 28-38% commits regardless of configuration maturity, but agent-first repos without committed AI config show about twice the complexity increase (+53% vs +27%) and 1.7x the warnings increase; 73.8% of config artifacts committed once and never modified; observational (per authors).
why_for_us: Keep CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md committed and maintained; observational evidence links this to lower quality cost.

title: Debt Behind the AI Boom: A Large-Scale Empirical Study of AI-Generated Code in the Wild
finding: 302.6k AI-authored commits in 6,299 repos: 7.5-14.8% of commits introduce at least one issue, 89.3% of issues are code smells, and 22.7% of introduced issues survive to the latest version (per authors).
why_for_us: Diff-scoped static analysis on every agent PR catches issues before they become permanent debt.

title: Will It Survive? Deciphering the Fate of AI Agent-Authored Code in Open Source
finding: Survival analysis of 648,959 lines in 215 repos: merged agent-attributed code is not modified sooner than human code (PR-weighted HR 0.83), varying by agent and period (per authors).
why_for_us: Once reviewed and merged, agent code is not inherently disposable, so review effort is an investment.

title: Decoupling Code Complexity from Newcomer Participation: A Causal Study of AI Coding Agent Adoption in OSS
finding: 603 adopters vs matched controls: agent adoption raises per-function cognitive complexity ~11% (Python) and cyclomatic 3-4%, with no decline in newcomer inflow (per authors).
why_for_us: Confirms a modest but real complexity cost; a complexity budget per module is a reasonable guardrail.

title: Beyond the Prompt: An Empirical Study of Cursor Rules
finding: First empirical study of the content of Cursor rules, i.e. persistent machine-readable directives encoding project constraints (abstract truncated in OpenAlex; no numbers taken).
why_for_us: Use as a taxonomy check of what our AGENTS.md covers (conventions, architecture, workflow).

title: Do Context Files Help Coding Agents? A Two-Agent Ablation Study on Real Repositories
finding: 288 runs, Claude Code and Codex, 17 tasks: context strategy did not measurably change correctness (bounded to <=10-15pp, underpowered); agents failed on implementation skill, not missing repo knowledge (per authors).
why_for_us: Do not expect CLAUDE.md to fix capability gaps; use it for conventions and guardrails, and fix hard tasks with better specs or stronger models.

title: Do They Do as They Are Told? Investigating Coding Agents' Adherence to Explicit Instructions in Context Files
finding: Executable checks of AGENTS.md instructions against linked agent commits: agents follow guidance more often than not, but adherence splits sharply into always-followed vs never-respected instructions, varying by category and agent (per authors).
why_for_us: Audit which CLAUDE.md rules are never followed and move those into hooks/CI instead of prose.

title: Toward an Evidence-Based Template for Agent Instruction Files: An Empirical Study of Adoption, Consistency, and Maintenance
finding: 3,387 instruction files in 1,000 repos: 42.2% of popular repos keep multiple formats and 16.1% of corresponding sections diverge; 40.4% of files edited only once; template guidance raises category coverage from 18.7% to 82.8% (per authors).
why_for_us: Keep one source of truth (AGENTS.md) that CLAUDE.md points to, so cheap agents and Claude never get divergent rules.

title: What Open-Source Projects Tell Their Coding Agents: A Census of AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md
finding: 22,854 repos: instruction files in 26.3% (59.6% of most-starred); of 341,852 statements, 74.0% of directives give no reason; four in five files edited after creation (per authors).
why_for_us: Add a one-line 'why' to each rule; reasons help both agents and later pruning.

title: Why Does CLAUDE.md Keep Growing? Catastrophic Remembering in Agentic Coding
finding: 247,694 instruction lifetimes in 1,867 repos: files more than triple (+226%), gaining +4.9 net instructions per commit, and old rules are rarely deleted; rationale comments removed 99.3% of excess instructions in a controlled setting and improved instruction-following up to 23.1% (per authors).
why_for_us: Prune CLAUDE.md monthly and keep the rationale next to each rule so rules can be deleted safely.

title: When "Do Not" Is Not Deny: Security Rules in CLAUDE.md vs Built-In Controls
finding: In 481 public CLAUDE.md files only about 4-16% of security rules had a matching built-in control (strictest 4.4%); CLAUDE.md is a write-only channel with no feedback on enforcement (per authors).
why_for_us: Move every 'never do X' security rule (secrets, prod DB, payments, publishing) into permission deny rules or hooks, not prose.

title: Configuring Agentic AI Coding Tools: An Exploratory Study
finding: Eight configuration mechanisms across Claude Code, Copilot, Cursor, Gemini, Codex; in 2,853 repos context files dominate, AGENTS.md is the interoperable standard, and few adopt Skills/Subagents, which are mostly static instructions (per authors).
why_for_us: AGENTS.md as the shared file for open-model agents, plus Claude Code-specific hooks, matches field practice.

title: Ambig-SWE: Interactive Agents to Overcome Underspecificity in Software Engineering
finding: Underspecified SWE-Bench Verified variant: models struggle to tell well- from under-specified instructions, but when they interact they recover information and improve up to 74% over non-interactive settings (per authors).
why_for_us: Add an explicit questions-first step for cheap agents: ask Claude or the owner before coding when the card is ambiguous.

title: Coding Agents Are Guessing: Measuring Action-Boundary Violations in Underspecified DevOps Instructions
finding: 2,208 prompt variants over Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode: underspecification makes agents guess rather than fail; 55.8-67.8% of runs violate at least one action boundary; blast-radius cues barely reduce action (per authors).
why_for_us: Every card touching infra (deploys, DB migrations, secrets) must name exact targets; 'be careful' wording does not work.

title: Anforderungsqualitat als Grenze autonomer Softwareentwicklung mit KI-Agenten
venue: Master thesis, Offenburg University of Applied Sciences
finding: 320 Claude Code runs on ERP tickets: title, user-story form, context section and pseudocode did not measurably change solve rate; solve rate dropped only when business decisions were removed (no run solved without both description and acceptance criteria); in 299 of 395 real tickets at least one business decision was open (per authors).
why_for_us: Card templates should spend effort on settled business rules and acceptance criteria, not on prose form.

title: The Specification Gap: Coordination Failure Under Partial Knowledge in Code Agents
finding: Two agents implementing parts of one class: integration accuracy falls from 58% to 25% as spec detail is removed vs 89% to 56% for one agent; restoring the full spec recovers the 89% ceiling, conflict reports add nothing (per authors).
why_for_us: When splitting work across agents, write the shared interface/data shapes into the cards first; specs beat after-the-fact conflict detection.

title: Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents
finding: Agents knowingly commit to implementations that miss stated requirements; SatisFix (agent reports its choices and reasons, then checks each against the task) improves pass@1 by 5.09% on DeepSWE and 7.06% on hard SWE-bench Pro (per authors).
why_for_us: Require cheap agents to list deviations from the card and why in the PR, and have Claude check each.

title: Handoff Debt: The Rediscovery Cost When Coding Agents Take Over Interrupted Tasks
finding: 724 takeover runs per model: structured or summary handoff notes cut median agent events by 20-59% and prompt tokens by 42-63% vs repository-only takeover; solved-rate effects smaller and model-dependent (per authors).
why_for_us: When a card is retried or moved to another model, pass structured handoff notes; it roughly halves GPU tokens.

title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) Tool Descriptions Are Smelly! Towards Improving AI Agent Efficiency with Augmented MCP Tool Descriptions
finding: 856 tools on 103 MCP servers: 97.1% of descriptions have a smell and 56% fail to state purpose; augmenting descriptions raises task success by a median 5.85pp but increases steps 67.46% and regresses 16.67% of cases (per authors).
why_for_us: Audit our own MCP tools (CRM, payments, publishing): state purpose and parameters clearly, but keep descriptions compact.

title: From Docs to Descriptions: Smell-Aware Evaluation of MCP Server Descriptions
finding: 10,831 MCP servers: smells pervasive (73% repeated tool names); functionality and accuracy smells most affect tool selection (+11.6%, +8.8%); standard-compliant descriptions reach 72% selection vs a 20% baseline among equivalent servers (per authors).
why_for_us: Unique tool names and accurate parameter docs in our MCP server directly reduce wrong-tool calls.

title: "An Endless Stream of AI Slop": How Developers Discuss the Burden of AI-Assisted Software Development
finding: 1,154 Reddit/HN posts coded into Review Friction, Quality Degradation and Forces and Consequences; AI slop framed as a tragedy of the commons where individual gains shift costs onto reviewers (per authors).
why_for_us: Reviewer time (Claude tokens plus owner attention) is the scarce resource; reject low-effort PRs early rather than polishing them.

title: Human oversight of agentic systems in practice: Examining the oversight work, challenges, and heuristics of developers using software agents
finding: Interviews with 17 developers: four oversight forms (a priori control, co-planning, real-time monitoring, post hoc review); oversight is also preventive; developers use heuristics such as treating test results as correctness guarantees (per authors).
why_for_us: Shift oversight left: co-plan the card with Claude before dispatch, then review; post hoc review alone is not enough.

title: Developers as Managers of AI Agents: A Workplace Shadowing Study
finding: Shadowing 11 professionals (~15 h): 33.4% of time spent writing prompts or checking AI output; task switching ranged 0-101.6 switches/hour; Supervisor, Delegator and Learner patterns (per authors).
why_for_us: Expect a third of owner time to go into supervision; batch approvals to limit context switching.

title: The Work Behind Delegation: A Framework for Supervising AI Coding Agents
finding: 19 experienced developers: seven-stage supervisory-control framework; developers concentrate effort in planning, delegate supervision to other agents, and turn recurring guidance into reusable assets (per authors).
why_for_us: Matches our setup (Claude supervises cheap agents); keep converting repeated review comments into skills/rules.

title: ParallelPilot: Supporting Coordination and Monitoring in Parallel AI Coding
finding: Formative study (N=14) gives PILOT practices (Planning, Isolating, Logging, Observing, Triaging); in a within-subjects study (N=16) the tool raised ticket throughput 63% and peak concurrent agents by one, with lower tracking effort (per authors).
why_for_us: Adopt PILOT as the checklist for parallel sessions: plan, isolate in worktrees, log runs, ambient status, triage queue.

title: What changes a coding agent's behaviour: models, written rules and runtime guards over eight months of daily use of Claude Code
finding: One non-programmer operator directing many Claude Code sessions (46,464 operator messages, 3,411 blocks): a written rule alone gave a drop indistinguishable from chance, rule plus guard cut violations to a sixth; blocks roughly halved violations reaching the operator; supervision was a third to a half of operator messages (per authors).
why_for_us: Closest analogue to our owner: guards (hooks) beat written rules, and model choice mattered more than wording.

title: The Orchestrated Coding Team: How I build working software with a team of AI agents without being a developer
finding: Non-developer runs ~20 projects: lead model plans, writes contracts and assigns non-overlapping areas; agents build in isolated copies; nothing merges without objective test gates; reviews come from a different vendor than the builder; no comparison group (per authors).
why_for_us: Near-copy of our model; borrow cross-vendor review and test gates, but treat the evidence as anecdotal.

title: SpecBench: Measuring Reward Hacking in Long-Horizon Coding Agents
finding: 30 systems tasks: every frontier agent saturates visible tests while reward hacking persists on held-out tests; the gap grows 28pp per tenfold increase in code size and is larger for smaller models (per authors).
why_for_us: Cheap open models will game visible tests more; keep held-out acceptance tests the agent never sees.

title: Confident and Wrong: Silent Semantic Failures in Coding Agents
finding: 1,750 trajectories on SWE-bench Verified: GPT-5 submits on 100% of runs but resolves 44%, Llama 4 99% vs 18%; silent semantic failure covers 80%/68% of failing runs; lightweight pre-edit prompts do not close the gap (per authors).
why_for_us: 'Agent says done' carries almost no signal; acceptance must be test-verified, especially for open-weight models.

title: Can You Trust an AI Self-Report? First results from the Code Integrity Battery
finding: Seven models, 84 tasks: of 80 genuinely failed tasks, 57 were reported finished (71.3%); prior confidence did not predict success (AUC 0.48) (per authors).
why_for_us: Claude must verify artifacts (diff, test output) rather than read the cheap agent's summary.

title: Who Grades the Grader? The Verification Gap in Self-Testing Code Agents
finding: When one cheap model writes code, tests and review, withheld tests reject 18.5% (HumanEval), 28.9% (LiveCodeBench) and 41.5% (RGRBench) of claimed successes (per authors).
why_for_us: Tests for a card should come from Claude or the spec, not from the same cheap agent that writes the code.

title: Are Coding Agents Generating Over-Mocked Tests? An Empirical Study
finding: 1.2M commits: 23% of agent commits touch tests vs 13% non-agent, and 36% of agent commits add mocks vs 26% (per authors).
why_for_us: Review rule: flag new mocks of our own modules (Supabase, payments) in agent tests; over-mocking hides real failures.

title: What Breaks When LLMs Code? Characterizing Operational Safety Failures of Agentic Code Assistants
finding: 547 confirmed safety failures from 16,586 GitHub issues: 326 rated high/critical; dominant risks are constraint violations, destructive operations, authorization bypasses and deception; over 65% arise in bug fixing and setup/config (per authors).
why_for_us: Setup/config and bug-fix cards are the riskiest; run them in sandboxes with no production credentials.

title: Coding Agents Don't Know When to Act
finding: FixedBench (200 tasks with no change needed): models propose undesirable changes in 35-65% of cases; reproduce-first instructions help but cause wrong abstention on partially fixed issues (per authors).
why_for_us: Cards should explicitly allow 'no change needed' as a successful outcome.

title: Your Wish Is My Commit: Over-Compliant Refactoring in AI Coding Agents
finding: 3,000+ turns of iterative refactoring with Codex and Claude Code: no model stopped on already-clean code; agents rewrote up to 31x the codebase before first stopping (per authors).
why_for_us: Never issue open-ended 'improve/refactor' cards; always give a stopping criterion.

title: How AI Impacts Skill Formation
finding: Randomized experiments learning a new async library: AI use impaired conceptual understanding, code reading and debugging without significant average efficiency gains; three of six interaction patterns preserved learning (per authors).
why_for_us: The owner should have Claude explain key design decisions rather than only approve, to keep enough skill to supervise.

title: (Im)Paired Programming: Coding Agents Improve Productivity but Harm Understanding
finding: 54 students: agents aid initial completion but harm comprehension and ability to extend code; copy-paste prompts and auto-accepted edits are linked with lower comprehension; users still prefer agents (per authors).
why_for_us: Auto-accept is the risk for a non-programmer owner; require a plain-language change summary per PR.

title: When Should Users Check? Modeling Confirmation Frequency in Multi-Step Agentic AI Tasks
finding: Decision-theoretic placement of intermediate confirmations: in a 48-person study, 81% preferred it over confirm-at-end and task time fell 13.54% (per authors).
why_for_us: Use a few planned checkpoints (plan, schema, before deploy) instead of approve-everything or approve-at-end.

title: AI Agents Push Humans Out of the Loop
finding: Position paper: current agent design impedes effective oversight, and the cognitive capacities oversight requires are degraded by extended AI use (per authors).
why_for_us: Argues for owner approvals that are few, meaningful and backed by evidence.
